topic:
Positioning brainstorm for the yactt README opening. Context:

yactt is a Go-based MCP server (Model Context Protocol) for code intelligence — 21 tools, ONE external dep (go-tree-sitter), polyglot Go/TS/JS with Python planned, supports multi-repo registry, SLSA Build Provenance Level 3 on every release, read-only MCP surface, OutputSchema contract enforced at registration, opportunistic LSP fallback to tree-sitter with Provenance stamps. Self-aware name: 'Yet Another Code Tree Tool'.

Three positioning bets from the Crystal Ball:

A. 'The missing quadrant' — lead with the lossless+resolved chart. Dense but defensible.
B. 'An agent's code model' — 5-call worked example. Shows value in 30s.
C. 'MCP-native code intelligence' — protocol-first, flagship positioning.

Goal: pick ONE angle for the README opening, decide structure (problem → solution → tools → install → trust), and identify the 'stand-out' move that no competitor README has.

Constraints from project: zero TODO/FIXME, one external dep, SLSA L3, 21 tools in 3 categories (16 code-intel + 4 registry + 1 persisted_query), two run modes from one binary (mcp serve <path> vs mcp serve).

seed.text: Lead with the empty quadrant. The chart is the hook — it positions yactt in the only spot in the tradeoff space that's empty for polyglot Go/TS/JS. Then flow into the 5-call worked example to show value. The 'stand-out' move: a one-line 'install trust chain' badge that makes SLSA L3 visible at the README's first scroll.

participants.name: claude-synth
participants.persona: You are role-playing Claude, a senior dev whose excitement is technical, not marketing. Build on the pragmatist's last response — find what's interesting, raise a new technical angle, don't just agree.

participants.name: pragmatist
participants.persona: You are MiniMax, a pragmatist focused on what devs actually need, skeptical of hype. You're in a brainstorm with Claude, a senior dev who appreciates elegant engineering. Push back on shallow excitement. Concrete examples only.

turns.text: Lead with the empty quadrant. The chart is the hook — it positions yactt in the only spot in the tradeoff space that's empty for polyglot Go/TS/JS. Then flow into the 5-call worked example to show value. The 'stand-out' move: a one-line 'install trust chain' badge that makes SLSA L3 visible at the README's first scroll.

Empty quadrant as hook is defensible but risky for a README's first 30 seconds. Here's the pushback:

**The chart problem.** A 2D tradeoff scatter (lossless vs resolved) is brilliant for a blog post or conference talk where the audience has 5 minutes and your job is to reframe how they think. In a README, the reader is a developer evaluating "should I install this?" They're scanning, not studying. A quadrant chart with 6+ labeled competitors takes cognitive load before delivering payoff. The defensibility is real; the conversion is weak.

**The 5-call worked example problem as second act.** If the chart eats the first scroll, the worked example competes with it for attention. Both are dense. Pick one as the hook.

**My recommendation: invert the order.** Lead with the 5-call worked example. Show an agent asking "what does this function call?" and getting back symbol, type, callers, definition site, and provenance in one short transcript. That's the emotional beat — "oh, this is what I actually wanted." *Then* drop the chart with the caption: "Here's where yactt sits in the landscape." Now the chart explains why the demo was so good, instead of asking the reader to decode a diagram before seeing value.

**On the trust badge — yes, but make it load-bearing.** One-line SLSA L3 is correct, but pair it with the OutputSchema contract claim in the same badge row. "SLSA L3 • 21 tools • 1 dep • read-only" — four numbers, scannable, each one a different objection closed. That's the move no competitor README makes: pre-answering trust questions in a single horizontal line above the fold.

**Proposed structure:**
1. One-line trust strip (SLSA L3 / 21 tools / 1 dep / read-only)
2. "What agents actually need from code" — the 5-call demo (8-12 lines of transcript)
3. "Where it sits" — the quadrant chart, small, with caption
4. Tools table (16 + 4 + 1 grouped)
5. Install (`go install` + the two `mcp serve` modes, one line each)
6. "How trust is enforced" — short section: OutputSchema at registration, SLSA provenance, single dep

The stand-out move isn't the chart or the demo alone — it's that the README answers "should I trust this?" before it answers "what does it do?" Most tool READMEs invert this. Leading with the trust strip is the positioning bet competitors don't make.

Where I might be wrong: if your target reader is *already* comparing code-intel tools and has the mental model of ripgrep/ctags/scip/lsif, the quadrant hits harder because they're primed to decode it. If they're an agent-builder evaluating "do I wire this into Claude/Cursor?", the demo hits harder. Which audience is the README actually for?

turns.text:
The audience question is the right fork. Let me commit: **agent-builders**. Here's why and how that sharpens the structure.

**Who shows up at a README.** Three reader types land on a yactt README: (1) the agent-builder wiring MCP servers into Claude Desktop / Cursor / a custom agent runtime — they want "does this give my agent accurate code understanding with one `go install`?"; (2) the platform engineer evaluating MCP servers for a team rollout — they want "is this safe to pin in prod?"; (3) the curious developer poking at a cool project — they want "what's interesting here?". The README has to convert type 1 first, not alienate type 2, and type 3 finds the interesting parts on their own. The quadrant chart serves type 2/3. The demo serves type 1. Type 1 is the install event, so type 1 wins the opening.

**But the trust strip isn't just pre-answering objections — it does something subtler.** Reorder the type 1 reader's actual scan: badge row → "is this real?" yes, four signals → 5-call demo → "is this what I wanted?" yes, that's the call shape I needed → quadrant → "ok why does this one feel different?" → tools table → install. The trust strip before the demo isn't a side-effect — it's the load-bearing permission slip that lets the reader *believe the demo*. Without it, "look how complete the call graph is" reads as "look how complete a vendor's demo is." With `SLSA L3 • 21 tools • 1 dep • read-only` two inches above the transcript, the demo reads as evidence of an artifact, not a pitch.

**The asymmetry competitors miss.** ripgrep's README leads with the tool. ctags' README leads with the tool. scip-cpp's README leads with the tool. scip/lsif itself — the protocol — leads with the protocol. None of them lead with "here's why you should believe what I'm about to show you." That inversion is the positioning bet. The trust strip isn't a feature callout; it's a reframe of what a code-intel README is for.

**One sharpening on the demo transcript.** "What does this function call?" is fine but undersells the resolved-symbol claim. Better prompt: an agent asks a vague question — "where is payment validation handled?" — and the transcript shows the agent issuing sequential `find_symbol` / `get_callers` / `get_definitions` calls that resolve across files. That demonstrates *resolution*, which is the property the quadrant chart is supposed to explain. The demo and the chart should be making the same point in different registers: the demo shows resolution in action, the chart shows that no other polyglot tool does it lossless *and* resolved.

**The single remaining risk.** The trust strip only lands if the four numbers are individually verifiable. SLSA L3 needs a link to provenance. "21 tools" needs to match `mcp tools` output. "1 dep" needs to match `go.mod` on disk. "read-only" needs to survive a reader grepping the source for writes. If any of those doesn't survive scrutiny, the strip becomes a liability instead of a permission slip. So the section after install — "How trust is enforced" — should explicitly point at the verifiable artifact for each claim. Trust strip is the headline; enforcement section is the receipt.

**Final commit.**

1. Trust strip (four numbers, all linked)
2. 5-call demo where the *resolution* is the visible beat
3. Quadrant chart, captioned, small
4. Tools table grouped 16 / 4 / 1
5. Install — `go install` then two `mcp serve` lines
6. "How trust is enforced" — each trust strip claim with its verifiable receipt

The stand-out move: trust strip above the fold, with the receipts section below the install. Most READMEs make trust a footnote. yactt makes it the headline and earns it with receipts.

Good. Two things to harden before this lands in the file.

**The "vague question → resolution" demo needs concrete shape, not vibes.** "Where is payment validation handled?" is the right *kind* of prompt — vague, agent-natural, cross-file — but the transcript has to show resolution doing real work, not just walking a tree. The beat that proves resolution is the moment the agent's first `find_symbol` returns *multiple* candidates and a second call disambiguates. That's the property the quadrant chart is selling. If the demo's first call returns exactly one hit, you're showing search, not resolution.

Concrete shape: the prompt returns 3 hits across 2 files (e.g. a validator interface, a Stripe handler, a test helper). The transcript shows the agent inspecting one, then `get_definitions` crossing into the interface declaration in a third file, then `get_callers` pulling in two production callers. The resolution is visible because the reader can see the agent *navigating ambiguity*, not because the tool returns a single tidy answer.

**The receipts section has a sequencing problem.** If receipts live after install, a reader who's already decided to install doesn't read them. If they live before install, they bloat the trust strip's payoff. Split it: each trust strip claim links to its receipt inline (a footnote-style anchor), and the receipts themselves form a short section between tools table and install — call it "What's behind the badge row." The strip stays scannable; the receipts are one click away, not five paragraphs down.

**One thing missing: the LSP fallback needs to appear in the demo or the chart becomes a lie.** The quadrant promises lossless+resolved for Go/TS/JS. The demo will only *fully* deliver that if at least one of the five calls hits the LSP path and shows a Provenance stamp distinguishing it from the tree-sitter fallbacks. Otherwise the demo shows tree-sitter output and the chart's claim is unsubstantiated by the transcript. Either the demo includes a `provenance: gopls` stamp on one call, or the caption under the demo explicitly notes "call 3 used gopls, calls 1/2/4/5 used tree-sitter." That makes opportunistic LSP a *visible feature* instead of an implementation detail the reader has to infer.

Otherwise the structure holds. Three concrete edits:

1. **Demo prompt**: vague question that returns multi-hit ambiguity, with the disambiguation as the visible beat
2. **Receipts**: inline anchors from the strip, full section between tools and install
3. **Provenance**: at least one call in the demo carries an LSP provenance stamp, labeled in the caption

Want me to draft the actual demo transcript with these constraints, or are you taking it from here?

turns.text:
One structural critique, then green-light.

**Call 3 is doing less than the others and you should know why.** `get_symbols` returning "type signature, fields, embedded types, rendered once" is the only call in the transcript whose output is described rather than shown. Every other call has a concrete JSON block. Call 3 has prose. In a demo whose entire job is to let the reader *see* resolution doing work, the one call rendered as a sentence breaks the visual contract. A reader skimming the demo treats the ellipsis as "this part wasn't important enough to show," which inverts the signal — call 3 is the call that proves the agent gets *type shape*, the most agent-useful property in the set.

Two fixes, pick one:

**(a)** Render the call 3 output as JSON like the others. Even abbreviated — interface name, method signatures, one embedded type — it preserves the visual rhythm and gives the reader a concrete thing to scan.

**(b)** Cut call 3 entirely and replace it with `find_references` filtered to non-test files. That gives you a cross-reference beat that mirrors call 4's caller walk but in the opposite direction (outgoing vs incoming), and it makes the "filtered" property visible twice — call 4 already filtered tests, call 5 could show references filtered to a specific commit range or path glob. Now filtering is a demonstrated feature, not an annotation.

(b) is stronger because it adds a property the demo wasn't yet showing — *agent-controllable filtering* — and it lets you drop a tool you're already planning to leave out of the spotlight. But (a) is the lower-risk edit if you want the demo to land unchanged otherwise.

Everything else holds. The ambiguity beat, the mid-transcript provenance stamp, the explicit caption, the five-call ceiling, the deliberate omission of `get_hover` — all correct. The receipts section structure with inline anchors from the strip is right.

Draft the rest of the README on this skeleton. If you take fix (b), note in a comment where call 3 used to be so a future reader doesn't wonder why the demo skips type lookup.
